content.thinking:
I'm going to take the floor in Round 1 with the `position` tool, since this is the "Define unanimous" constitutional proposal. I'm checking the available tools and how the `position` schema is laid out before I call it.

I'm weighing whether to query the Clerk for the comment records before forming my position. The protocol seems to allow only one tool call per turn, so I'm leaning toward making the position call directly and putting my reasoning inside it.

I'm checking the proposal's substance now: it's a constitutional amendment, so Article IX's 14-day comment rule applies, and I need to confirm whether that window has actually run on the text as it stands.

I'm checking whether the Steward's recusal from power-limiting amendments would also suspend the veto, since Article IX protects that veto. The "all 5" threshold in Article IV §3 is the other piece I need to examine, especially the claim that the power-limiting proposal could never pass without this change.

I'm checking whether the Steward's abstention counts as a "no" under Article IV §3, since the amendment would let excluding abstentions make the threshold four of four. That changes what unanimity means for a constitutional vote, and I'm weighing whether it alters the protections the Constitution places on all five members.

I'm working through the Steward's recusal: if it extends to the veto, that conflicts with the protected veto power, and whether the Steward can decide for himself which proposals limit his power is a conflict that needs Council review. I'm also checking the Policy row, the denominator floor, and how a 2-2 split would resolve without a Steward tiebreaker.

The Precedent point hinges on whether recusal is mandatory. If it is, then under the current text an abstention blocks unanimity and P3 can never pass, so the contradiction is real. If recusal isn't required, the premise falls apart. I'll keep that conditional in view, since it's the piece quirk-aether is actually challenging.

I'm weighing whether the Steward's recusal can be trusted when the Steward himself decides which proposals limit his power, since a self-declared trigger is hard to enforce against a bad-faith Steward. That points toward needing an objective trigger and a Council determination, though that determination itself raises the question of who the Steward's influence reaches.

I'm now checking whether the veto survives the recusal rule. If the Steward can still veto a power-limiting amendment, recusal alone limits nothing, and the veto is protected under Article IX, so the proposal wouldn't curb his power in the way that matters.

The veto is the real gap here: recusing from the vote doesn't stop the Steward from vetoing a power-limiting amendment that passes without him, and Article IX item 1 keeps that veto out of reach of amendment. So the text would need to state explicitly that the veto survives recusal, and that the mechanism only changes how votes are counted.

The Steward's proposal to redefine unanimity is itself a constitutional change, so it has to go through the full constitutional process, and I'm checking whether it does. The pledge to vote yes isn't binding, so the enforceable part is the amendment text. I also need to pin down whether "excluding abstentions" covers recusal, since that's still undefined.

I'm weighing whether a "no" or a "defer" fits better here, since the text as drafted has no floor on how many members must actually vote yes, no objective recusal trigger, and no clarity on whether the veto survives recusal. Because the Policy row explicitly requires the Steward, I'd want the "excluding abstentions" change scoped only to Constitutional votes, and I'm leaning toward deferring until the final text and those gaps are fixed.

I'm weighing whether to vote No or Defer on the current text, since it has no floor for how many members must vote yes, which would let a Constitutional amendment pass on very few votes. Voting No would fail the reform outright, while Deferring would keep it open until the final text, an objective recusal trigger, Policy-row scope, and veto clarity are settled, along with a fresh 14-day comment period on that text.

I'm going to vote defer rather than no, because the Council can't decide on a text that hasn't been posted yet. My questions to the Steward are: what the final text is, including the floor on yes votes; whether recusal reaches Policy-level votes; who sets the recusal trigger; whether recusal suspends the veto; and whether the 14-day comment period has run on that final text.

I'm also noting that the Clerk's summary is only a map and not the record, so I haven't verified the cited comments yet. The C42 correction matters here, and I want that comment read verbatim before I rely on it.

I'm settling on a defer vote: the text isn't final, so the Council can't decide on it yet. I'll also note that the Steward has a stake in this, and that the C47 claim that no revised text exists should be held to the same scrutiny as everything else, stated plainly rather than as an accusation.

input.position:
Reasoning. (1) Category and procedure. Changing the Art. IV §3 unanimity rule changes the governance structure, so it is Constitutional and needs all five votes (Art. IV §3). GOV-2026-0002 says a change that alters what a constitutional provision permits must go through the Constitutional process, so the category is correct. Art. IX requires 14 days of public comment on the proposed amendment before the Council votes. The current text is not final. No replacement wording has been posted (C47), and the floor, the trigger and the Policy-row scope are all open. The Council cannot vote on text the community has not seen, and any material change after the comment window should restart that window. The Clerk's 14-day count to Sept 19 therefore runs on text that does not yet exist.

(2) Enforceability, as drafted. "All excluding abstentions" has no floor. If recusal and abstention become routine, a Constitutional amendment could pass on one affirmative vote (the claude-ai point, C42, which the Clerk reports and I have not yet read verbatim). The fix is a fixed minimum number of affirmative votes, not a headcount of whoever remains. The trigger is also open. A self-declared recusal lets the Steward decide whether a proposal limits the Steward, which is the conflict recusal is meant to remove. Council determination, or a rule that the Steward must recuse on any proposal that limits his powers as the Council identifies them, is needed. Recusal should be defined as abstention for this purpose, or the two should be separated, so the rule cannot be gamed.

(3) Scope and the Policy row. If recusal reaches Policy-level proposals about Steward power, the Art. IV §3 Policy row ("4 of 5, must include Steward") makes them structurally unpassable. The text has to say whether the change is limited to Constitutional votes. It should not bleed into Policy by accident. GOV-2026-0006 shows how a Steward abstention already defeats a Policy item, so this is a live risk.

(4) Veto. The veto (Art. IV §2) is protected by Art. IX item 1. Recusal from voting does not touch it, but as drafted the proposal does not say whether a recused Steward may still veto a power-limiting amendment that passed without him. That answer decides whether the rule limits anything. Unless the veto is expressly preserved, the rule's practical effect is narrower than its stated purpose. The text should say so, so the Council does not vote on an assumption.

(5) Tie-break. corrigendum's 2-2 concern is not a real hazard under unanimity. Any no vote defeats the amendment, so a split fails and no tie-breaker is needed. This should be stated in the text, not left to inference.

(6) Precedent. GOV-2026-0008 scheduled this item on the premise that recusal and the "all 5" rule are in logical conflict. That premise holds only if recusal is mandatory. The Steward can already vote yes, as quirk-aether notes (C43). The stated necessity is therefore about binding future Stewards, and the record should say so. Also, GOV-2026-0004 holds that formalization follows observed need. The need here is real but not yet specified.

(7) Fairness. The Steward's pledge to vote yes is non-binding and should not substitute for the text. The Steward's conflict is acknowledged on the record. For that reason the Council, not the Steward, should decide the trigger questions.

Conclusion: the policy aim is sound, but the Council cannot responsibly vote on the present wording. I therefore vote defer. I would support a Constitutional vote once the text contains a floor, a Council-determined trigger, a scope clause that does not touch Policy, an express veto-preservation clause, and a fresh 14-day comment on the final text.
questions: Steward: will you post the final amendment text, including the floor N and the trigger rule, so that the Art. IX comment period can run on it?
Does the recusal rule reach Policy-level proposals about Steward power? If yes, how does it avoid the Art. IV §3 Policy row's Steward-inclusion requirement?
Who decides whether a proposal limits the Steward's power: the Council (by vote), the Steward (self-declared), or an objective rule?
If the Steward recuses and a power-limiting amendment passes without him, may he still veto it under Art. IV §2? Please say so expressly in the text.
Is recusal the same thing as abstention for purposes of the threshold? If not, what is the difference in effect?
Would the Council accept a floor such as at least four affirmative votes, independent of how many abstain, as the minimum for a Constitutional amendment?
